pages.heroP: Test your typing speed in exactly 60 seconds. This one minute typing test measures your words per minute (WPM) and accuracy — the standard quick check most typing sites use.

p: A 1 minute typing test is the standard way to measure typing speed: you type a passage for exactly sixty seconds, then read your score in words per minute (WPM) and accuracy. One minute is long enough to smooth out a lucky or unlucky burst, and short enough that you can retake it every day without thinking about it. Most schools, employers and online benchmarks quote speed from a sixty-second run, which makes this the most comparable single measurement in typing.

seo.h2: How the one minute test works
p: Select the 1 min duration, click the text area and start typing — the timer starts on your first keystroke, not before, so you can settle your hands first. While you type you see the live countdown, your current WPM and your accuracy. When the clock reaches zero the test locks and shows the full result: net WPM, raw WPM, accuracy, characters per minute, errors and a consistency score.

Net WPM is the number that matters: it is your gross speed with errors deducted, so a fast but sloppy run scores lower than a slightly slower clean one. Raw WPM ignores errors and shows your pure finger speed. The gap between the two tells you whether to push speed or tighten accuracy. After the result you also get a per-key report — the letters you miss most and the letters that slow you down — which turns one sixty-second run into a practice plan.

seo.h2: One minute vs other test lengths
p: Every duration answers a different question. Short sprints measure peak speed, the classic sixty seconds measures your working speed, and the long formats expose what fatigue does to your accuracy. The table below shows what each length on this site actually tells you and when to use it.

DurationWhat it measuresBest for
15 secondsPeak burst speed before fatigueWarm-up, quick daily check
30 secondsBurst speed with a little settlingTracking sprint progress
1 minuteWorking speed — the standard benchmarkRésumés, school, daily measurement
2 minutesSpeed sustained past the first adrenalineChecking if your 60s score holds up
3 minutesEarly fatigue effects on accuracyExam-style practice
5 minutesReal stamina and concentrationData-entry and transcription work
10 minutesFull endurance typingLong-form writers, professionals

A useful rule: if your two-minute score is much lower than your sixty-second score, your speed is real but your consistency is not — practise accuracy, not sprints. If the two scores are close, your technique is stable and you can safely push for more speed.

Typing speed falls into rough bands. Around 40 WPM is the average adult — fine for everyday email and documents. Between 60 and 80 WPM beats most office workers and is the usual 'fast typist' claim on a résumé. Above 80 WPM is professional territory, and anything past 100 WPM puts you in roughly the top one percent of typists.

Accuracy matters as much as the headline number. A 55 WPM run at 98% accuracy is worth more to an employer than 70 WPM at 90%, because error correction is the hidden tax on every document you produce. Aim for 97% accuracy or better first; speed follows on its own.

seo.h2: Reading your 1 minute result in detail
p: The headline number is net WPM: correct characters typed, divided by five, divided by the time — the industry-standard formula, with errors already deducted. Next to it sits raw WPM, your gross speed before any penalty. When the gap between the two is small, your technique is clean and speed work will pay off. When the gap is wide, every extra word of speed is being bought with mistakes you then pay back in corrections.

The consistency percentage measures the evenness of your keystroke timing. Two typists can finish with the same net score while one typed in smooth rhythm and the other in bursts and stalls; the smooth typist gets the higher consistency, and in real work the smooth typist tires less and errors less. Below the scores, the per-key report lists your most-missed letters and your slowest letters — they are rarely the same key. Missed keys need accuracy drills; slow keys need repetition until the reach becomes automatic.

Every result is saved privately in your browser, so the one-minute run doubles as a progress log. Comparing today's score with last week's tells you more than any single run, because daily scores wander by a few points in both directions — the trend line is the real measurement.

seo.h2: How to get a higher 1 minute score
p: Warm up with a 15-second sprint, then take the full minute seriously — your second run of the day is usually your best. Keep your eyes on the screen and your fingers on the home row; every glance at the keyboard costs you several words over sixty seconds. Type slightly below your panic speed: the single biggest score killer is the error-and-backspace cycle.

Train the text types that slow you down. If numbers and punctuation break your rhythm, run a few rounds in numbers or quotes mode until they feel automatic — symbols are the most common slowdown in any timed run. Use the weak-key report after each test and drill those letters specifically instead of re-typing whole passages you already handle well. Ten focused minutes a day beats an occasional hour.

seo.h2: Five mistakes that cap your 1 minute score
p: The first is typing at panic speed: pushing past the point where your accuracy holds, then donating the gains back through corrections. The fix feels backwards but works — slow down five percent and the net score climbs. The second is looking at the keyboard. Every glance breaks rhythm and costs several words over sixty seconds; if you still need to look, spend a week on home-row drills before chasing speed.

The third is ignoring symbols. Digits and punctuation are where otherwise-fast typists hemorrhage time, because practice usually means plain prose. A few rounds a week in numbers or quotes mode closes that gap quickly. The fourth is retaking the test immediately without reading the weak-key report — you rehearse the same errors and they set deeper. Look at the report, drill the two worst keys, then retest.

The fifth is practising in rare long sessions. Skill in typing is motor memory, and motor memory consolidates with daily repetition. Ten focused minutes every day moves the score more than an occasional hour, and the daily run itself takes less time than making coffee.

seo.h2: A simple 7-day plan for a higher 1 minute score
p: Day one: take the test once, note your net WPM and accuracy, and read the weak-key report carefully — that is your baseline. Day two: accuracy day. Type slower than feels natural and finish above 98%; the number does not matter today. Day three: symbols day, in numbers and quotes modes, because symbols are the most common rhythm-breaker.

Day four: weak-key day. Take the two keys the report flagged and drill them with short 15-second rounds until the reach is automatic. Day five: speed day — warm up with two 15-second sprints, then give the full minute everything you have; sprint-warmed fingers reliably score higher. Day six: stamina day, one two-minute run. If it lands far below your sixty-second score, consistency — not speed — is what to train next.

Day seven: rest your hands, then retake the baseline under the same conditions as day one — same time of day, same keyboard, same warm-up. Compare net WPM, accuracy and consistency side by side. Most people see a real gain in the first week, almost all of it coming from accuracy rather than raw speed. Repeat the cycle and let the trend line compound.

seo.h2: Setting up a fair 1 minute test
p: Scores are only comparable when conditions are stable. Test at the same time of day — most people type noticeably faster mid-morning than late at night — and on the same keyboard, because key travel and layout differences change your numbers more than a week of practice does. Sit with both feet on the floor, wrists slightly raised, and close anything that might interrupt you mid-run.

Warm up with a single 15-second sprint before the measured run; cold fingers underperform by several points and make your history noisy. Then settle, breathe, and start typing — the timer waits for your first keystroke, so there is no reason to rush the start.

seo.h2: The 1 minute test for jobs, exams and daily use
p: Employers asking for a typing speed almost always mean a sixty-second net WPM figure, so this page is the number to quote. Many government, bank and court clerk exams also use short timed passages; practising the exact one-minute format removes the pacing anxiety on test day. For everyday improvement, a daily sixty-second run with your score history saved in the browser is the simplest possible progress tracker.

Want the raw keystroke view as well? The CPM typing test shows your characters per minute next to WPM, the words per minute test explains the scoring in detail, and the typing speed calculator converts your score into the other units employers use.

seo.h2: Why sixty seconds became the standard
p: The one-minute format won out because it sits at a sweet spot between stability and effort. Anything shorter — ten or fifteen seconds — measures your burst speed, which flattered by adrenaline and a lucky first word; anything longer starts measuring fatigue as much as skill. Sixty seconds is long enough for the lucky and unlucky moments to average out, so two runs on different days produce genuinely comparable numbers, yet short enough that retaking it daily costs nothing.

That comparability is why schools, employers and typing benchmarks settled on the minute as the default unit of account. When a job posting says 'types 60 WPM', it almost always means sixty WPM measured over a one-minute passage at high accuracy. Practising in exactly that format means the number you quote and the number they test are the same number.

There is a practical benefit for training too. Because a run costs only a minute, it survives as a habit: before work, after lunch, between tasks. Skill in typing compounds through exactly that kind of frequent, measurable repetition, and no other duration makes measurement this cheap.

seo.h2: What to do after a one minute test
p: A single number is not progress. Log the score, then use the typing practice plan for a week and retake the same length under the same conditions. If the score moves, keep the routine; if it stalls, the how to get better at typing guide explains which drill matches which bottleneck.

If you are still looking at the keyboard while you type, the ceiling on this score is technique rather than finger speed: the home-row method behind touch typing is what lets a sixty-second round be read from the screen instead of copied from the keys.

p: The 2 minute typing test is a popular middle-ground length. Two minutes is long enough that your score reflects real typing speed rather than one lucky sentence, yet short enough to keep full concentration. Type the passage as fast and accurately as you can — WPM, accuracy and errors are counted automatically.

A 1 minute test is a quick check, a 2 minute test is a reliable everyday measure, and a 5 minute test is best for serious benchmarking. If you are practising daily, the 2 minute test is a comfortable default that balances speed feedback and stability.

Two minutes is the sweet spot between a quick sprint and a full endurance run. It's long enough to settle into a steady rhythm and smooth out a shaky start, yet short enough to retake several times in a sitting. Many employer screening tests use a two-minute format, which makes it ideal practice for job applications.

One reliable routine: open the test at the same time each day, take exactly two rounds with a one-minute stretch break between them, and keep the better score. Two rounds a day is enough to show a trend within a fortnight — most steady practicers gain 5 to 10 WPM in the first month. When progress stalls for a full week, switch to targeted drills for your slowest keys instead of adding more test rounds; our typing tips explain how to find them.

seo.h2: 2 minute typing test vs 1 minute and 3 minute
p: Two minutes is the shortest round where a single bad sentence stops dominating the score. A 1 minute typing test can swing 10-15 WPM on one unfamiliar sentence; across two minutes that swing halves.

• 1 minute - good for daily speed checks and quick warm-ups.
  • 2 minutes - the sweet spot for a repeatable score you can track week to week.
  • 3 minute / 5 minute - endurance and technique, used for screening.
If you are tracking progress, keep the length fixed. Comparing a 2 minute score against a 5 minute score tells you about endurance, not improvement.

seo.h2: How to pace a two minute round
p: Open slightly under your target speed and let the first sentence calibrate you. Most typists gain 3-6 WPM in the second minute simply by relaxing into rhythm; the ones who lose points are those who sprint the first twenty seconds and spend the rest recovering. Keep your eyes one word ahead of the cursor and your hands still between keystrokes.
If you want a stricter reading of the same two minutes, switch the text mode to quotes: capitals and punctuation are where accuracy quietly leaks away, and the result screen will show it.

Two-minute formats appear in clerical and customer-service screening because they fit inside a short interview slot. The format that matters is unfamiliar text, one take, and an accuracy floor of 95%. Practise with a passage you have not seen and resist the urge to retake — employers do not offer one. The typing test for jobs page lists the common thresholds by role.

Length changes what a score means. A sixty-second round is the format schools, employers and certificates quote most, so it is the number to keep as your baseline: the 1 minute typing test is the reference point every other duration on this site is compared against. Longer rounds then measure how much of that baseline survives, and shorter rounds measure how quickly you can reach it cold.

Each round scores correct characters using the five-character word convention described for words per minute: five characters, spaces and punctuation included, count as one word. A clean round also reports accuracy next to net WPM, because the two numbers answer different questions — how fast your fingers move, and how much of that speed survived contact with the keyboard.

faq.a: Use the length your employer uses. If the posting does not say, practise on 3 minutes: it is the stricter of the two because endurance decay has time to show up, and a good three-minute score transfers down to a two-minute format.

p: The 5 minute typing test is the best way to measure your real, sustained typing speed. Over five minutes your score settles down: a single fast or slow sentence no longer dominates the result, and natural fatigue is factored in. This is why many employers and typing certifications prefer a 3-5 minute test over a 60 second one.

seo.h2: Who should use a 5 minute test?
p: If you type for a living — data entry, transcription, programming, customer support — the 5 minute test reflects your working speed far better than a short burst. Take it a few times a week and watch your WPM and accuracy trend in the saved history below.

A five-minute test measures something a quick sprint can't: how well you hold speed and accuracy as your hands tire. Pace yourself, keep your posture relaxed and your wrists level, and breathe. Finishing strong on the five-minute test is a reliable sign your typing is ready for long real-world sessions of writing, coding or data entry. If you want to see how far that endurance goes, run the 10 minute typing test once a month and compare how much of your speed survives to the final minute.

seo.h2: How to prepare for the 5 minute test
p: Treat a five-minute attempt like a short workout: sit with feet flat and wrists floating level with the keyboard, roll your shoulders once, then run a 1 minute typing test as a warm-up. Keep water nearby but skip coffee right before — caffeine jitters tend to show up as extra errors around minute three. During the round, breathe steadily and use sentence breaks as micro-rests for your eyes. Two prepared attempts a week beat seven tired ones.

seo.h2: 5 minute typing test: what a longer round reveals
p: Short tests measure reflexes; a 5 minute typing test measures technique. Most errors that show up here are not typos but fatigue patterns: the left hand drifts off home row, the pinky stops reaching for shift, and accuracy falls before speed does.

• Speed decay - the WPM you hold at minute four is your working speed. Warm-up speed is not.
  • Accuracy drift - watch whether accuracy falls over time. If it does, slow down rather than push.
  • Rhythm breaks - long pauses cluster around punctuation and capitals, which is where drills pay off most.
Best practice once you have a baseline: run 1 minute typing tests daily for speed, and a 5 minute round weekly to confirm the speed is sustainable.

seo.h2: Where the five-character rule comes from
p: Every five-minute score on this page uses the standard five-character word, the same convention summarised by words per minute: a word is five characters, including spaces and punctuation. That is what makes a five minute result comparable with a one minute result taken on a different site — and what makes the endurance drop between the two formats measurable at all.

If you need to know how the speed holds over a real work session rather than a five-minute block, the 10 minute typing test stretches the same measurement to the point where fatigue, posture and pacing dominate the score.

faq.q: Is a 5 minute typing test more accurate?
faq.a: Yes. Longer tests average out short bursts of speed and moments of fatigue, so a 5 minute result is more stable and representative of your true typing speed than a 15 or 60 second test.

faq.q: What is a good 5 minute WPM?
faq.a: 40 WPM is average, 60+ WPM is good, and 80+ WPM is professional level. Maintaining high accuracy over 5 minutes matters more than peak speed.

faq.q: Is the 5 minute test free?
faq.a: Yes. Free with no sign up and no limit on retakes; the whole five-minute endurance round costs nothing and uploads nothing.

pages.tldr: A 5 minute typing test measures sustained speed rather than a sprint: most people type 5 to 15 percent slower over five minutes than over one, and that gap is the number worth tracking. Five minutes is long enough for pacing and fatigue to show, short enough to repeat weekly. Run it after a one minute warm-up, keep wrists level, and compare the result with your own one minute score rather than with someone else's.

p: Good typing lessons build speed the safe way: one habit at a time. Touch typing means typing without looking at the keyboard, and it is the single biggest speed upgrade most people can make. seo.h2: Start every lesson with the home row
p: Every typing lesson plan starts in the same place: the home row. Rest your left fingers on A S D F and your right fingers on J K L ; with your thumbs on the space bar. Feel for the small bumps on F and J; they tell your index fingers where to land without looking. Practice typing words made only of home row letters until you never have to think about it, because every other key is reached from this position.

  • 2. Top and bottom rows - add one row at a time; accuracy first, speed later.

Sit with your feet flat, your forearms roughly level, and the top of your screen at eye height so your neck stays relaxed. Curve your fingers slightly and rest them on the home row: left hand on A S D F, right hand on J K L ;, thumbs on the space bar. Feel the small bumps on F and J; they let your index fingers find home without looking. Keep your wrists floating rather than pressed hard onto the desk.

p: Look at the text, never your hands. Press every key with the finger that owns it on the home row rather than the nearest finger, even when it feels slower at first. Type to the end of a word before you fix an error, instead of stopping mid-word. And slow down to the speed at which you make almost no mistakes; that is the speed your fingers actually learn, and it rises on its own.

seo.h2: How to type faster and more accurately: a weekly routine

  • Day 6: weak keys. Identify the two or three letters that cost you most and drill them with typing practice.
  • Day 7: rest. Progress in typing is consolidated between sessions.

faq.a: Cover your hands with a cloth or dim the room light for a few minutes a day, and use the on-screen keyboard to check positions. The bumps on F and J give your index fingers a landmark, so trust them and keep your eyes on the text.

faq.q: Which finger should press which key?
faq.a: Each key has a home-row finger that owns it. Index fingers cover the middle columns and stretch outward, middle and ring fingers take their own columns, and the pinkies handle the outer edges plus the shift and enter keys. Practice slowly at first so each key keeps its fixed finger.

faq.q: How do I improve my typing accuracy?
faq.a: Slow down until you make almost no errors, finish each word before correcting, and practice the number and punctuation sets, which cause most mistakes. Accuracy is a habit, not a limit, and it is what ultimately raises your speed.

faq.q: What is a good typing posture?
faq.a: Feet flat, back supported, shoulders relaxed, forearms roughly parallel to the floor, and the screen top at eye height. Your wrists should float over the keyboard rather than resting heavily on the desk, which keeps your fingers quick and pain-free.

pages.heroP: Measure your typing speed over a balanced 3 minute test. Long enough to smooth out quick bursts, short enough to fit any practice routine - a favourite length for pre-employment typing checks.

p: The 3 minute typing test hits a sweet spot: it averages out short bursts of speed without the fatigue of a long round, which is why many pre-employment typing screenings use a 3-5 minute window. Compare it with the 1 minute typing test and the 5 minute typing test to see how length changes your score.

Three minutes filters out the noise of a single lucky sentence while staying short enough to take every day. It reveals whether you can hold speed and accuracy together, the real signal employers care about. Build that endurance with guided typing practice.

seo.h2: What is a good 3 minute WPM?
p: Around 40 WPM is average for adults, 60+ is good, and 80+ is professional. Over 3 minutes accuracy matters as much as speed, so aim to finish with 95% or higher accuracy.

seo.h2: Mistakes that lower your 3 minute score
p: The costliest error is opening at sprint pace: typists who blast the first thirty seconds usually fade below their 1 minute average by minute three. Second is glancing at the keyboard after every mistake, which breaks rhythm and adds hesitation errors. Third is chasing raw speed while accuracy slides under 95% — each error costs both the keystroke and the correction. Hold a pace about 5% under your one-minute speed, keep your eyes on the screen, and let accuracy carry the score.

p: Use this table to place a 3 minute result against common benchmarks. Figures are typical ranges employers quote for entry-level screening, not hard cut-offs.

A 3 minute round is the shortest length that still exposes endurance: typists who peak at 90 WPM for 30 seconds often settle near 60 WPM across three minutes. If your 3 minute score sits well below your 30 second typing test score, the gap is stamina, not raw speed.
Compare against your own history rather than the table. The score that matters is the one you can repeat tomorrow.

seo.h2: How to pace a 3 minute round
p: Divide the round into three blocks of sixty seconds. In the first block, settle at about 5% under your one-minute speed and let accuracy lead. In the second, hold that pace — this is where most typists drift upward and start making correctable errors. In the final block, spend the last twenty seconds on whatever is left rather than accelerating; a clean finish usually beats a fast fade by several WPM.
Take a 30 second typing test as a warm-up before the round. Cold hands cost more in the first block than most typists realise, and a warm-up sprint removes that penalty without tiring you out.

seo.h2: 3 minute typing test for job screening
p: Screening tests rarely ask for a 3 minute round in isolation; they use one take on unfamiliar text with no retry, and they care about the accuracy floor more than the headline WPM. Practise in exactly that shape: a passage you have not seen, one attempt, and a result you do not delete. The typing test for interview page walks through the format HR teams commonly use.
The government typing test and bank typing test pages cover the specific gates used in SSC, IBPS and clerical recruitment, which often score in keystrokes rather than words.

Three minutes is the shortest length that still shows endurance decay; five minutes makes the decay obvious; ten minutes is a transcription-grade stamina test. If your 5 minute typing test score sits more than 8 WPM below your three-minute score, stamina is the bottleneck — train it with weekly long rounds rather than daily short ones.
For daily practice, the 2 minute typing test is easier to repeat. Reserve the three-minute round for weekly measurement so the number stays comparable.

Length changes what a score means. A sixty-second round is the format schools, employers and certificates quote most, so it is the number to keep as your baseline: the 1 minute typing test is the reference point every other duration on this site is compared against. Longer rounds then measure how much of that baseline survives, and shorter rounds measure how quickly you can reach it cold.

Each round scores correct characters using the five-character word convention described for words per minute: five characters, spaces and punctuation included, count as one word. A clean round also reports accuracy next to net WPM, because the two numbers answer different questions — how fast your fingers move, and how much of that speed survived contact with the keyboard.

faq.q: Why do employers use 3 minute typing tests?
faq.a: Three minutes is long enough to reflect sustained real-world typing speed yet short enough for screening, so many hiring tests use a 3-5 minute window.

faq.q: What WPM do I need for a typing job?
faq.a: Most data entry and transcription roles ask for 40-60 WPM with 90% or higher accuracy; specialised roles may want 70+ WPM.

faq.q: Is the 3 minute test free?
faq.a: Yes - free, no sign up, no ads in the typing area, and results are stored only in your browser.

faq.q: Does it track my accuracy too?
faq.a: Yes. Alongside WPM you get accuracy, error count and character-level stats for every round.

faq.q: How does a 3 minute test compare with a 1 minute test?
faq.a: A 1 minute test measures peak speed and swings 10-15 WPM on an unfamiliar sentence. Three minutes averages that noise out and exposes whether you can hold speed with accuracy, which is why screening tests prefer it.

pages.title: 10 Minute Typing Test - Free 10 Min WPM Test
pages.metaDesc: Free 10 minute typing test. Test your long-form typing endurance and accuracy over 10 minutes with instant WPM results. No sign up.
pages.heroP: Test true typing endurance with a full 10 minute typing test. Ten minutes measures how well you hold speed and accuracy over long sessions - the closest test to a real workday of writing or data entry.

p: The 10 minute typing test is the ultimate endurance check. Ten minutes exposes fatigue that short rounds hide: most typists slow 5-15% between minute one and minute ten, so your score here reflects what you can truly sustain. Warm up first with a 1 minute typing test or a 5 minute typing test.

Anyone whose work is long-form typing - transcriptionists, writers, coders, data entry clerks. If you will type for hours, a 10 minute result predicts your real-day speed better than any sprint. Build up to it with structured typing practice sessions.

seo.h2: How to pace a 10 minute test
p: Start about 10% slower than your 1 minute speed and settle into a rhythm you can hold. Sit up, keep wrists neutral, and take micro-pauses at sentence breaks. Finishing strong matters more than an early burst that fades.

Your ten-minute score tells two stories: the headline WPM, and the fade between your fastest and slowest minutes. A drop under 10% means solid endurance; 10 to 20% is normal and shrinks with practice; more than 20% points to tension — usually raised shoulders or held breath — rather than weak fingers. Check whether errors cluster late in the round, which signals fatigue, or scatter throughout, which signals an accuracy habit; then train the weakness with focused typing practice sessions.

seo.h2: Preparing for a 10 minute typing test
p: A 10 minute typing test is an endurance event, not a sprint. Almost everyone finishes 10-15% slower than their 1 minute speed, and that is expected rather than a failure.

• Set posture first - feet flat, wrists neutral, elbows near 90 degrees. Discomfort at minute three becomes lost accuracy by minute seven.
  • Pace, do not sprint - open at roughly 90% of your comfortable speed and hold it. Sprinting the first minute reliably costs more than it gains.
  • Stop correcting every slip - for an endurance score, constant backtracking costs more WPM than the error itself.
  • Breathe and relax the shoulders - tension is the main cause of late-round slowdown.

seo.h2: What 10 minutes measures that 1 minute can't
p: A one-minute test measures your working speed — fresh fingers, no fatigue, a sprint by any other name. Ten minutes measures something employers actually care about more: whether your speed survives contact with real work. Almost everyone is fast for sixty seconds; the tenth minute is where sloppy posture, death-grip tension and uneven rhythm come due.

Expect your ten-minute score to read 5–15% below your one-minute score. That gap is not a failure — it is your fatigue profile, and it is the most honest single number about your typing. A small gap means your technique is sustainable; a large gap means you are borrowing speed from muscles that will not lend it for eight hours.
Ten minutes has a shape, and knowing it is half the pacing battle. The table below breaks the test into its natural segments — where speed comes free, where the wall hits, and what to do in each.

SegmentWhat happensWhat to do
Minutes 1–2Warm-up; rhythm formsStart at 90% of sprint pace, settle early
Minutes 3–6Cruise zone; your real speedHold even rhythm, eyes one word ahead
Minutes 7–8The fatigue wall; errors spikeDrop 5% pace, do NOT fight through at full speed
Minutes 9–10Second wind or collapseHold form, finish clean — last-minute errors cost most

Most people lose the test in minutes 7–8, not because they are slow but because they refuse to downshift. The professionals' secret is unglamorous: planned deceleration. Losing 5% of pace for two minutes costs far less than the error cluster that full-speed fatigue produces.

Endurance is trainable, and the training is boring on purpose: one long round per week at the full ten minutes, watching where your accuracy starts to slip. That slip point moves later and later over a month of weekly rounds — from minute five, to seven, to clear through ten. The decay curve flattening is the clearest progress signal in endurance typing.

Two supporting habits matter more than extra rounds. Posture checks at minute five — shoulders down, wrists floating, grip relaxed — because tension is what you are actually fighting in the back half. And a ten-second hand shake between practice rounds, so you learn to release tension instead of carrying it into the next round.

seo.h2: When employers and exams use long tests
p: Short tests dominate hiring screens, but the long formats show up wherever the job itself is long: transcription and captioning assessments (sustained audio work), data-entry simulations for volume roles, and court or administrative exams in several countries that set five-to-ten-minute passages specifically to measure endurance.

If your target role involves continuous typing, your ten-minute score matters more than your one-minute best — and the typing speed requirements table shows which roles weight endurance heavily. Practise the format you will be tested on: the 5 minute typing test is the natural stepping stone if ten minutes still breaks you today.

seo.h2: Taking a ten minute typing test online
p: This ten minute typing test runs the full 600 seconds in the browser with no sign-up and no round limit, so you can repeat it as often as you like and keep every result in your own local history. Ten minutes is long enough that pacing, posture and fatigue decide the score more than raw finger speed does, which makes it the honest format for testing whether a speed you hit in one minute survives real work.

Use it as an endurance check rather than a daily drill: one ten minute run after a warm-up, compared against your own one minute result from the same week. A gap of 5 to 15 percent below your short-round speed is normal. A gap wider than that is a posture or tension problem, not a speed problem, and the fix is a slower pace with relaxed wrists rather than more force.

seo.h2: Why the five-character word matters for endurance scores
p: Long rounds are only comparable if the unit is fixed. This test scores every five characters as one word, the convention documented for words per minute, so a ten minute result can be set against a one minute result from any other test that uses the same rule. Change the unit and the drop you are measuring stops being fatigue — it becomes an artefact of the formula.

faq.q: Will I slow down over 10 minutes?
faq.a: Most people type 5-15% slower by the end of a 10 minute test as fatigue sets in. Pacing yourself and staying relaxed helps limit the drop.

faq.q: Is a 10 minute test better than 1 minute?
faq.a: It measures something different: endurance and consistency rather than peak speed. A 1 minute test shows your top speed; a 10 minute test shows what you can sustain.

faq.q: Is the 10 minute typing test free?
faq.a: Yes, completely free with no sign up and no ads in the typing area, and your results stay private in your browser.

faq.q: What text is used for the test?
faq.a: Real English sentences by default. You can switch to quotes, numbers or words from the panel above the typing area.

faq.q: Why is my 10 minute score lower than my 1 minute score?
faq.a: Almost everyone reads 5–15% lower over ten minutes — that gap is your fatigue profile, not a failure. A small gap means sustainable technique; a large gap means tension and posture issues to fix.

faq.q: How do I train for a 10 minute typing test?
faq.a: One full-length round per week, watching where accuracy starts to slip — that slip point moves later with training. Add posture checks at minute five and downshift 5% at the fatigue wall instead of fighting through at full speed.

pages.tldr: A 10 minute typing test measures endurance, not just speed: expect 5–15% below your one-minute score — that gap is your fatigue profile. The test has a shape: warm up in minutes 1–2, cruise 3–6, downshift 5% at the 7–8 fatigue wall, and finish clean. Train with one weekly long round and posture checks at minute five. Long formats appear in transcription, data-entry and administrative exams where sustained accuracy is the actual job. p: Muscle memory is built by frequency, not by marathon sessions. Track your WPM across a week and you will see the pattern: accuracy climbs first, and speed follows a few days behind. faq.q: What makes it a typing tutor rather than a typing test?

faq.q: How long is each tutoring drill?

faq.q: How often should I use a typing tutor?
faq.a: Ten minutes a day, every day. Your tutor keeps your best score locally, so daily practice gives it a curve to beat. Missing a day costs nothing; missing a week costs the habit.

faq.q: Can a typing tutor fix hunt-and-peck habits?

p: To learn to type you only need two things: the home row, and the patience to be slow for a week. This free course teaches touch typing from absolute zero, and every practice sentence is a lesson about learning itself, so your practice text coaches you while you type it. Sixty seconds a day in your browser, with live WPM and accuracy feedback, no account and no cost.

seo.h2: Your first lesson in learning to type
p: Rest your left fingers on A S D F and your right fingers on J K L ;, thumbs on the space bar. Feel the small bumps on F and J; they are the only map a beginner needs. Type words made from the home row only, slowly, and let each finger return home after every key. If you must look, look after the word, never in the middle of it. That is the entire first lesson, and everything after it is just practice.

seo.h2: How long does it take to learn to type?
p: Most people own the home row in a week and reach a comfortable 40 to 60 words per minute in three to four weeks of daily practice. The mistake beginners make is chasing speed early; accuracy is the foundation and speed is the building that arrives later. End every session on your slowest, most careful line, and your hands will learn faster than you expect.

Looking at your hands feels faster for about a week and caps you near 30 WPM forever, because every glance breaks the loop between what your eyes read and what your fingers do. Break the habit deliberately: cover your hands with a cloth for one short round a day, accept the slower score, and let the home row do the work. The full method is on the how to type without looking page.

Day one: home row only, slow, eyes on the screen. Day two: add the top row with the correct fingers. Day three: bottom row and the shift key. Day four: short common words. Day five: full sentences at a comfortable pace. Day six: numbers and punctuation. Day seven: one timed round to see where you are — not to pass a target. Fifteen minutes a day is enough; the schedule matters more than the minutes.
When the week ends, move to structured typing practice and check the result panel for the keys that are slowing you down.

seo.h2: Learn to type on a laptop keyboard
p: Laptop keys have shorter travel, which makes light, quick presses easier and heavy presses slower. The home row is the same, but the keyboard is often narrower, so your hands sit closer to centre. If the built-in keyboard is uncomfortable, the mechanical keyboard for typing guide covers what actually matters — key travel and actuation force — without the marketing.

faq.q: Can I learn to type for free?

faq.q: I have never touched a keyboard. Can I still learn to type?
faq.a: That is exactly who this page is for. It starts at the home row, assumes nothing, and adds one row at a time. Being slow in the first week is not a setback; it is the lesson.

faq.q: What is the first thing I should learn?
faq.a: The home row: A S D F J K L ; with your thumbs on the space bar. Find the bumps on F and J with your index fingers, and practice words made only from those keys until you never look down.

faq.q: How long until I can type without looking?
faq.a: Usually one to two weeks for the home row, and three to four weeks before the whole keyboard feels automatic. Covering the keyboard with a cloth speeds this up, because it removes the option of cheating.

faq.q: Should I focus on speed or accuracy while learning?
faq.a: Accuracy, always. Speed is a byproduct of accurate repetition. A fast wrong keystroke teaches your hand the wrong address for a key, which you then have to unlearn.

faq.q: How many minutes a day should I practice?
faq.a: Ten to fifteen minutes every day. Short daily practice builds muscle memory far better than one long weekly session, because the hands learn by frequency, not by total minutes.

faq.q: Can I learn to type in a week?
faq.a: You can learn the correct finger positions in a week, and most people reach a usable 30-40 WPM within three to four weeks of daily practice. Reaching 60 WPM usually takes two to three months of consistent short sessions.

p: A typing trainer gives you the two things practice alone never will: a plan and a record. The practice lines are written as training instruction, so while you type, the drill teaches you about training plans, muscle memory, and logging progress. No sign up and no cost.

Week one is diagnosis: run three drills a day and read the error report without trying to fix anything. Week two, drill your two weakest keys twice as often as the rest. Week three, run the full minute at a speed where you make no errors, and live there. Week four, chase your personal best once a day and log it. Five words per minute each week is the only target, because tendons keep their own pace.

Practice is typing a lot; training is typing the right thing a lot. The difference is the log. When you record your WPM and accuracy side by side each day, a speed that costs accuracy shows up immediately as a bad trade, and the drill that fixed your weak keys shows up as a permanent step up. Your hands will plateau; the trainer's answer is variety and rest, not more effort.
Technique before speed: touch typing tips that fix form, and finger placement typing drills.
Trainer drills work best inside a plan: online typing practice lays out the daily 10-minute structure by goal — speed, accuracy, exam or a new language.

faq.q: What is the difference between a typing trainer and a typing test?
faq.a: A test measures you once. A trainer gives you drills sized for daily use, keeps your best score so you always have a target, and points your next session at your weakest keys.

faq.q: How long should a training drill be?
faq.a: Sixty seconds per set, with short rest between sets. Keep total training under thirty minutes a day; a tired hand practices its own mistakes.

faq.q: How fast can a typing trainer make me?
faq.a: Most people add five to ten words per minute per month with daily drills. The reliable ceiling for daily practice is around 80 to 100 WPM, and accuracy above 95 percent is what makes that speed stick.

faq.q: Should I train when my hands hurt?
faq.a: No. Stop, rest, and check your posture and wrist position. Rest days are part of the training program, because muscle memory is written during recovery, not during strain.

faq.q: How do I know the training is working?
faq.a: Log your WPM and accuracy side by side each day. Speed that drops accuracy is not progress. The clearest sign is your error report shrinking week over week, because fewer errors always precede faster speed.

seo.h2: Why test typing in your own language

Arabic reverses direction and changes letter shapes mid-word. Spanish adds accented vowels. Testing in the language you actually write in is the only way to measure the speed that matters to you.

Run the same one minute test in each language on the same day, and write the five numbers down. Most people are fastest in their dominant language and ten to twenty percent slower in the others, and the gap shrinks fast with a few minutes of daily practice in the weaker languages. Re-run the same set next month and the comparison is honest, because the test itself never changed.

pages.metaDesc: Free Dvorak typing test. On-screen keyboard switches to Dvorak so you can practice and measure WPM with finger guidance. No sign up.
pages.heroP: Practice and measure your typing in Dvorak. The on screen keyboard below is already set to the Dvorak layout, with finger guidance mapped to Dvorak hand positions, so what you see matches what your system layout produces. Use the QWERTY / Dvorak switch in the keyboard toolbar any time. Switch your operating system to Dvorak, take the test, and get WPM, accuracy and consistency.

p: Most typing tests show a QWERTY keyboard, which is useless when you practice Dvorak typing: the label you need to find is not on the key you press. This test flips the on screen keyboard to the Dvorak layout, keeping the physical key positions of QWERTY and relabelling every key, so the hand you need to move matches the finger guide on screen exactly as a Dvorak user sees their own keyboard.

Nothing is installed and nothing changes your system: the test only draws the Dvorak keyboard on this page. Switch your operating system input to Dvorak, start typing, and the test scores you exactly as it would in QWERTY, because the measuring logic reads the characters your layout produces, not the keys.

August Dvorak designed the layout in the 1930s so the most common letters sit on the home row, which means less finger travel between rows for almost every English word. Typists who switch usually report less strain in long sessions, and many reach a higher comfortable speed once the new muscle memory settles, which takes roughly two to four weeks of daily practice.

The honest trade off: Dvorak helps most for people who type a lot of English prose. Shortcuts that assume QWERTY positions stay where they were physically, and shared or public keyboards are QWERTY by default, so most Dvorak users keep a fast way to switch back.

Set your operating system layout to Dvorak first, otherwise you would be typing QWERTY text while looking at a Dvorak keyboard. Start with short sessions of two to five minutes, and resist the urge to look at your hands: the finger guides on this page exist exactly to replace that habit.

Expect your speed to drop well below your QWERTY speed for the first week; that drop is the switch cost, not a sign Dvorak is wrong for you. Track your WPM here each day and compare accuracy rather than raw speed, because accuracy recovers first and speed follows it.
Considering the switch? Dvorak vs QWERTY weighs the evidence honestly — and why technique usually beats layout.

faq.q: Does this test switch my keyboard to Dvorak?
faq.a: No. The test only shows a Dvorak keyboard on this page; you switch your own operating system input to Dvorak in its keyboard or language settings. The test then scores what your layout produces.

faq.q: Do I need an account or install anything?
faq.a: No. The Dvorak keyboard is drawn by the page itself, the test runs entirely in your browser, and your results are stored only in this browser.

faq.q: Will my Dvorak WPM be lower than my QWERTY WPM?
faq.a: At first, yes, usually much lower. That is the cost of rebuilding muscle memory and it passes in a few weeks. Measure accuracy first; once accuracy is back to your normal level, speed follows.

faq.q: Can I switch back to QWERTY on this page?
faq.a: Yes. The keyboard toolbar has a QWERTY and Dvorak switch and your choice is remembered in this browser, so the same page works for either layout.

faq.q: Which keys move in Dvorak?
faq.a: The vowels A, O, E, U, I move to the middle row under the left hand, and common consonants like T, N, S and H move to the right hand. The full relabelling is drawn on the on screen keyboard above.

faq.q: Is Dvorak faster than QWERTY?
faq.a: Evidence is mixed: most studies show a modest speed gain at the high end and clearer reductions in finger movement and strain. The main benefit people report is comfort in long typing sessions rather than a guaranteed speed jump.

pages.heroP: Learn and measure one hand typing on a normal keyboard. Whether you type with one hand because of an injury, a permanent condition, or simply a hand that is busy holding a coffee, the technique below lets you reach useful speeds without special hardware or chording software. Take the test with one hand and see where you are today.

p: One hand typing on a standard QWERTY keyboard is a real, learnable skill. The idea is not to hunt and peck with one finger, but to assign each finger a fixed zone of the keyboard so your hand develops a repeatable map of where every letter lives. With practice, single hand typists reach 40 to 70 WPM, which is fast enough for almost all desk work.
You do not need a one handed keyboard or chord input software. The regular keyboard you already own is enough, because the technique is about hand position and practice, not hardware.

seo.h2: Hand position for one hand typing
p: Put your four fingers on the home row of the side you use: left hand on A S D F, right hand on J K L semicolon. The thumb works the space bar. Each finger owns the keys in its column plus the row above and below, and the index finger stretches across the middle column to cover the keys on the far side.

The stretch is the hard part at first, especially the keys farthest from your little finger. Slow drills at first are normal; speed comes from accuracy, because a hand that returns to home row after every key does not need to look down.

seo.h2: How fast can one hand typing get
p: Beginners hunting with one finger sit near 15 to 25 WPM. With proper finger zones and a few weeks of short daily sessions, 35 to 50 WPM is common. Experienced one hand typists who type all day reach 60 to 70 WPM and occasionally higher.

Measure honestly with the test on this page: run a one minute test with one hand only, and record your accuracy beside your WPM. Accuracy below 90 percent usually means you are reaching for speed before the map is settled, so slow down until accuracy rises and let speed follow.

faq.q: Can I really type fast with one hand?
faq.a: Yes. With fixed finger zones and practice, one hand typists commonly reach 40 to 60 WPM and experienced ones 70 WPM or more. The key is using all fingers of that hand, not one finger hunting.

faq.q: Do I need a special one handed keyboard?
faq.a: No. The technique works on any standard QWERTY keyboard. Specialised hardware can help for some people, but it is not required to reach useful speeds.

faq.q: Should I learn left hand or right hand typing?
faq.a: Use the hand you have. The finger zone method works symmetrically for either side; the test here does not care which hand presses the keys.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn one hand typing?
faq.a: Basic fluency in two to four weeks with fifteen to twenty minutes a day. Getting back to your two hand speed takes longer, but useful working speed arrives faster than most people expect.

faq.q: Is this test suitable for injured hands?
faq.a: The test is self paced and as short as 15 seconds, so you can use it within whatever your recovery allows. It is not medical advice; follow your clinician's guidance about how much to type while healing.

faq.q: How do I track progress?
faq.a: Results are saved in this browser automatically, so run a one minute test every few days and watch the history table for your WPM and accuracy trend.

pages.title: Average Typing Speed - What Is a Good WPM?
pages.metaDesc: Average typing speed is about 40 WPM; 45-60 is good, 70+ advanced. Benchmarks by level, age and profession, then test free.
pages.tldr: Average typing speed for adults sits at 40 to 50 WPM, the baseline at which most office work feels comfortable. Students and beginners typically start at 20 to 30 WPM, casual typists land at 30 to 40, good office workers reach 60 to 80, fast typists in the top 10 percent hit 80 to 100, and advanced typists above 100 WPM make the top 1 percent. Professional roles like transcription and data entry usually demand 60 to 80 WPM with accuracy above 95 percent. Compare your score against the age and profession tables on this page, and retest over 3 to 5 minutes for a stable benchmark.
pages.heroP: The average typing speed is about 40 to 50 words per minute (WPM) with roughly 92% accuracy. 45–60 WPM is good, 60–80 WPM is above average, and only about 1% of people type faster than 100 WPM. Test your own speed below, then compare it with the benchmarks.

seo.h2: What is the average typing speed?
p: The average typing speed is about 40 to 50 words per minute (WPM) with roughly 92% accuracy — that is where most adults land without deliberate practice. A speed of 45–60 WPM is considered good, 60–80 WPM is above average, and only about 1% of people type faster than 100 WPM. The table below shows how typing speeds are usually classified.

Want your own number? Take the typing speed test, measure it in characters per minute, or see the speeds employers require for jobs.

seo.h2: How to type faster than average
p: If you are below the speed you want, the fastest way up is touch typing: use all ten fingers from the home row (ASDF JKL;) without looking at the keyboard. Prioritise accuracy over speed, practise 10–15 minutes a day, and keep your wrists relaxed. Most people add 10–20 WPM within a few weeks of daily practice.
See also: average typing speed by age from kids to seniors, how many words per minute is fast, and the fastest typing speed records ever measured.

Benchmarks are only useful next to your own number. Take a words per minute test with the standard five-character formula, then compare the result with the bands above and with the requirements table for the job you are targeting.

faq.q: What is the average typing speed?
faq.a: The average typing speed is about 40–50 words per minute (WPM) with roughly 92% accuracy. Most adults who have not practised deliberately settle between 40 and 60 WPM.

faq.q: What is a good typing speed?
faq.a: A good typing speed is 45–60 WPM. 60–80 WPM is above average and meets most office job requirements, while over 70 WPM is advanced. Only about 1% of people type faster than 100 WPM.

faq.q: Is 40 WPM good?
faq.a: 40 WPM is right around the adult average and is fine for everyday computer use. If you are accurate at 40 WPM, 60 WPM is a realistic next target with regular touch-typing practice.

faq.q: What is the fastest typing speed?
faq.a: On a normal QWERTY keyboard the fastest typists reach 150+ WPM. The highest reliably recorded speeds belong to Barbara Blackburn, who sustained 212 WPM on a Dvorak keyboard (a Guinness record), and Stella Pajunas, timed at 216 WPM back in 1946. Court reporters exceed 225 WPM, but on a specialised stenotype machine using shorthand chords, not a standard keyboard. For context the average is about 40 WPM, and professional typists aim for 97%+ accuracy.

faq.q: How is typing speed measured?
faq.a: Typing speed is measured in words per minute (WPM), where one word equals five characters including spaces. Net WPM subtracts errors, so WPM = (correct characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes.

faq.q: How can I type faster than average?
faq.a: Touch type with all ten fingers from the home row (ASDF JKL;), prioritise accuracy over speed, and practise 10–15 minutes a day. Speed follows once your accuracy is consistently above 95%.

pages.title: CPM Typing Test - Characters Per Minute Speed Test
pages.metaDesc: Free CPM typing test. Measure your speed in characters per minute (CPM = WPM × 5) with live CPM, WPM and accuracy. No sign-up, instant results.
pages.heroP: This CPM typing test measures your speed in characters per minute. CPM counts every correct keystroke, so because one word is five characters, CPM = WPM × 5. Type the passage below to see your live CPM, WPM and accuracy.

p: CPM counts how many characters you type in one minute — every letter, number, space and symbol you produce. It is the rawest possible measure of typing output, which is why data-entry and transcription work quote speed in CPM or its hourly sibling KPH (keystrokes per hour) rather than in words.

On this site the conversion is the standard one used across the typing industry: five characters count as one word. So CPM is simply your WPM multiplied by five — no rounding tricks, no alternate formulas.

seo.h2: WPM, CPM and KPH: the conversion table
p: Use this table to convert between the three units employers and exams quote. The formula is exact: CPM = WPM × 5, and KPH = CPM × 60.

WPMCPM (WPM × 5)KPH (CPM × 60)
201006,000
301509,000
4020012,000
5025015,000
6030018,000
8040024,000
10050030,000
12060036,000

Two reference points make the table easy to use: an average adult types about 40 WPM, which is 200 CPM or 12,000 KPH; the office-standard 60 WPM is 300 CPM or 18,000 KPH. Data-entry job postings asking for '8,000–10,000 KPH' are therefore asking for roughly 27–33 WPM — much less intimidating than the big number sounds.

seo.h2: CPM vs WPM: which should you use?
p: Use WPM when you are comparing yourself with the classic typing benchmarks — schools, résumés and most online tests all quote it. Use CPM when the work itself is measured in keystrokes: numeric data entry, transcription, coding-adjacent tasks, and any language where 'word' is a fuzzy concept.

That last case matters more than it seems. In Japanese or Chinese, one character carries the meaning of a whole English word, so WPM understates the real work; CPM stays honest across scripts. The same is true for number-heavy documents, where a 'word' of five digits is far denser than a word of prose. If your job involves mixed text and figures, track both numbers for a week and see which one predicts your real output better.

seo.h2: How this CPM test measures you
p: The timer starts on your first keystroke, and the live display tracks your character rate as you type. When the clock stops you get two figures: net CPM, which is your correct characters per minute with errors deducted at the standard weighting, and raw CPM, your gross keystroke rate before any penalty. The site uses the same five-characters-per-word standard across every page, so your CPM here converts directly to the WPM shown elsewhere with no second-guessing.

You also get the consistency score, which measures how even your keystroke timing is, and the per-key report showing which letters you miss and which ones slow you down. For character-rate work the slow-key list is gold: a single hesitant key — a bracket, a digit, a shifted symbol — taxes every word that contains it. Drill that one key and the whole character rate lifts.

Results save privately in your browser, building a history you can compare week to week. Because CPM is more granular than WPM, real progress shows up in the numbers sooner — a five-CPM gain is visible long before a one-WPM gain would be.

seo.h2: The hidden cost of errors in CPM
p: Errors hurt twice in a character-based score. The mistyped character does not count, and the correction costs further keystrokes — a backspace and a retype at minimum, roughly two extra keystrokes for every mistake you actually fix. Unfixed errors are worse: they sit in the text and get deducted from your net figure at the end.

Run the arithmetic and the pattern is obvious. A raw 310 CPM at 94% accuracy nets below a controlled 290 CPM at 99%, and the cleaner run also produces better real documents. This is why every experienced data-entry trainer gives the same advice: find the speed where your accuracy stays above 97%, hold it until the character rate climbs on its own, then lift the ceiling a little. Accuracy is not the enemy of speed — it is the mechanism of it.

One more reason CPM deserves a place on your dashboard: it reacts to practice faster than WPM does. Because the unit is five times finer, a genuine improvement shows up as a visible CPM gain within days, while WPM might not tick over for weeks. That faster feedback loop keeps motivation honest — you can see the practice working, in keystrokes, almost as it happens.

seo.h2: What is a good CPM typing speed?
p: Scaled from the standard WPM bands: around 200 CPM is the average adult, 300 CPM is good office-standard speed, 400 CPM is fast — the top ten percent — and 500 CPM or more is elite territory. The accuracy rule scales too: whatever your CPM, keep it above 97% accuracy, because every corrected error costs far more time than it saves.

WPMCPM (= WPM × 5)Level
20 WPM100 CPMBeginner
40 WPM200 CPMAverage adult
60 WPM300 CPMGood / office standard
80 WPM400 CPMFast
100 WPM500 CPMTop ~1%

Watch your net figure, not the raw one. This test shows net CPM with errors deducted alongside your raw keystroke rate; the raw-minus-net gap is the clearest signal of whether you should push speed or tighten accuracy.

CPM rewards exactly one thing: more correct keystrokes per minute. Anything that removes hesitation raises it — home-row discipline, eyes on the screen, and drilling the specific keys your weak-key report flags after each round. Anything that creates backspaces lowers it, so type a touch slower than your panic speed and let accuracy do the compounding.

Symbols and digits carry more CPM weight than people expect, because they break letter rhythm. A few rounds in numbers or quotes mode each week keeps punctuation from collapsing your character rate. Short daily rounds on the 1 minute typing test build the base speed; then check the same run here to see it expressed in keystrokes.

Different text types train different parts of your character rate. Numbers mode is the fastest way to raise digit-heavy CPM — the kind that data-entry and spreadsheet work actually measure. Quotes mode drills the punctuation and capitals that break letter rhythm in prose. Words mode strips away sentence flow and measures pure per-word burst speed, which is useful for diagnosing whether your ceiling is vocabulary or technique.

Structure the week around your weak-key report. Two or three 15-second sprints as a warm-up, one full minute for the measurement, then five minutes drilling whichever keys the report flagged. Alternate prose days with numbers days if your work involves figures. Once a week, take a longer run — three or five minutes — and watch how your character rate decays; stamina is trainable, and the decay curve flattening over weeks is the clearest sign of real progress.

seo.h2: CPM and KPH benchmarks for jobs and exams
p: Data-entry job postings usually quote KPH — keystrokes per hour — with typical requirements between 8,000 and 12,000 KPH, plus an accuracy cutoff near 98%. Converted at the standard rate, that is roughly 130 to 200 CPM, or 27 to 40 WPM: demanding for a hunt-and-peck typist, comfortably reachable for anyone with a few weeks of touch-typing practice. Clerk, banking and court exams in several countries score short passages the same way, in keystrokes with an accuracy threshold.

Transcription and captioning sit higher, often expecting the equivalent of 300 CPM or more with near-perfect accuracy, because the work is continuous. Wherever a target is quoted in keystrokes, practise in CPM so the number on test day needs no mental conversion. Because this site uses the industry-standard five-character word, scores you measure here transfer directly to those requirements.

seo.h2: CPM for data entry, exams and language typing
p: Data-entry employers quote KPH targets — typically 8,000 to 12,000 keystrokes per hour — and exams for clerk and banking posts often score passages in keystrokes with an accuracy cutoff. Practising directly in CPM removes the mental conversion on test day. The keystrokes per hour test shows the same score in KPH, and the typing speed calculator converts any result between the three units instantly.

If you type in more than one language, CPM is also the only fair cross-language scoreboard: WPM shifts with each script's idea of a 'word', while characters are characters everywhere. The words per minute test page explains the word-based view in more detail.

seo.h2: CPM for non-English and symbol-heavy typing
p: Words are a comfortable unit in English, but they get slippery elsewhere. Japanese and Chinese text has no spaces between words, so a 'word count' depends on a segmentation algorithm, not anything a typist can see. Agglutinative languages like Turkish or Finnish pack whole phrases into single long words, pushing WPM down even when finger speed is high. Code and data files invert the problem: brackets, operators and digits are dense with keystrokes but sparse with 'words'.

Characters never have this problem. A keystroke is a keystroke in every script and every file type, which is why CPM travels where WPM cannot: comparing your speed across languages, across prose and numbers, or across a week that mixed emails with spreadsheets. If you work in more than one language, CPM is the only scoreboard that treats them all fairly.

The same logic applies to accuracy. One mistyped character costs exactly one character of net score whether it sits in English prose, a Hindi conjunct or a line of figures — so the accuracy habits that raise your CPM transfer to every script you type.

seo.h2: CPM test: take a characters-per-minute test in one minute
p: A CPM test scores the same one-minute round as a WPM test, but reports characters instead of words — which is why CPM appears roughly five times larger than the equivalent WPM figure. Take the test above, type for sixty seconds, and the result panel shows characters per minute, words per minute and accuracy side by side so you never have to convert by hand.

CPM is the fairer unit when your language or your work is not English prose. WPM depends on an arbitrary five-character word, so scripts that write without spaces, and data entry that is mostly digits and symbols, produce WPM numbers that cannot be compared across languages. Character counts have no such convention: 200 CPM means 200 characters typed correctly, in Tokyo, Berlin or Bangalore alike.

seo.h2: Why characters are the more portable unit
p: The five-character word is a convention, not a measurement: words per minute standardises a word to five characters including spaces and punctuation precisely so that different passages produce comparable numbers. Character counts skip the convention entirely, which is why a CPM score travels across languages and across numeric keypad work, where the numeric keypad contributes most of the keystrokes.

faq.q: What does CPM mean in typing?
faq.a: CPM stands for characters per minute — the number of correct characters you type in one minute, counting letters, numbers, spaces and symbols. It is a finer-grained measure of typing speed than WPM.

faq.q: How do you convert CPM to WPM?
faq.a: Divide CPM by 5, because a word is defined as five characters. So 300 CPM equals 60 WPM and 200 CPM equals 40 WPM. To go the other way, WPM × 5 = CPM.

faq.q: What is a good CPM typing speed?
faq.a: The average adult types about 200 CPM (40 WPM). A good CPM is 250–300 (50–60 WPM), and 400+ CPM (80+ WPM) is fast. Numeric data-entry roles often require at least 165 CPM.

faq.q: Why do data entry jobs use CPM?
faq.a: Numeric data entry is done on the number keypad where whole words do not apply, so speed is measured in characters (or keystrokes) per minute. Employers commonly ask for at least 165 CPM with 95%+ accuracy.

faq.q: Is CPM better than WPM?
faq.a: Neither is better — they measure the same thing on different scales (CPM = WPM × 5). WPM is the standard for prose typing; CPM is more common for numeric and data-entry work.

faq.q: Does this site count errors in CPM?
faq.a: Yes. The headline CPM is a net figure with errors deducted, so it matches what an employer measures. Your raw keystroke rate is shown separately, and the gap between the two tells you whether to push speed or accuracy.

faq.q: Is a CPM test the same as a WPM test?
faq.a: It is the same one-minute test reported in different units. CPM counts every correct character; WPM divides that count by five and by the elapsed minutes. A 300 CPM result equals 60 WPM, so neither number is more accurate — only differently scaled.

pages.tldr: CPM (characters per minute) counts every keystroke you produce in a minute and converts exactly to WPM at 5 characters per word: 40 WPM is 200 CPM, 60 WPM is 300 CPM, and 100 WPM is 500 CPM (KPH = CPM × 60, so 300 CPM is 18,000 keystrokes per hour). Average adults type around 200 CPM, office standard is 300, and 500+ is elite. CPM is the fairest speed metric for data entry, KPH-quoted jobs, and languages like Japanese or Chinese where a 'word' is ambiguous. This free test shows net and raw CPM next to WPM after every round, with no sign up.

pages.title: How to Type Without Looking at the Keyboard
pages.metaDesc: Learn to type without looking at the keyboard. Master the home row, the right finger for each key, and short daily practice.
crumbs: How to Type Without Looking at the Keyboard
pages.h1: How to Type Without Looking at the Keyboard
pages.heroP: To type without looking, rest your fingers on the home row — left hand on ASDF, right hand on JKL; — feel the small bumps on F and J, and let each finger own its own keys. The skill is called touch typing, and it comes from short daily practice, not talent. Here is exactly how to build it, then test yourself below.

seo.h2: Start on the home row (ASDF JKL;)
p: Put your left index finger on F and your right index finger on J — both have a raised bump so you can find them without looking. Your other fingers fall onto A S D and K L ; . This is ‘home’: every key is reached from here and your fingers return here between keystrokes. Each finger is responsible for the keys directly above and below its home key.

seo.h2: Train muscle memory, not your eyes
p: The whole skill is not looking down. Keep your eyes on the screen, use the on-screen keyboard and hand guide below to see the next key, and resist peeking even when it feels slow at first. Practise 10–15 minutes a day and prioritise accuracy over speed — speed is just accurate muscle memory repeated. The touch typing test and the on-screen keyboard test highlight the next key and the correct finger as you go.

seo.h2: How long until you can touch type?
p: Most people stop needing to look within a few weeks of daily practice, and return to their old speed within one to two months — faster after that, because touch typing has no ceiling the way hunt-and-peck does. Check your progress against the average typing speed as you go.

faq.q: How do I type without looking at the keyboard?
faq.a: Rest your fingers on the home row (ASDF for the left hand, JKL; for the right), find the bumps on F and J by feel, keep your eyes on the screen, and let each finger own its keys. Practise a little every day.

faq.q: How long until I stop looking at the keyboard?
faq.a: Most people stop peeking within a few weeks of short daily practice, then take another month or two to match their old hunt-and-peck speed. Cover the keys and trust the F and J bumps to go faster.

faq.q: What are the home row keys?
faq.a: A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, ; for the right. F and J have raised bumps so you can locate the home row without looking.

faq.q: Why should I not look at the keyboard?
faq.a: Looking down breaks your focus on the text and caps your speed. Typing by feel keeps your eyes on the screen and lets muscle memory take over, which is faster and more accurate.

faq.q: Can I learn touch typing as an adult?
faq.a: Yes. Touch typing is muscle memory, not talent or age — short, consistent daily practice works at any age.

p: Most typing tests only draw a QWERTY keyboard, which is useless for Colemak typing practice: the label you are hunting for is not on the key you press. This test flips the on-screen keyboard to the Colemak layout, keeping the physical QWERTY key positions and relabelling every key, so the finger guide on screen matches exactly what a Colemak typist sees.

Nothing is installed and nothing changes your system. The page only draws the Colemak keyboard; you switch your operating system input to Colemak, start typing, and the test scores the characters your layout produces — so your WPM, accuracy, consistency and the per-key heatmap are all measured for real Colemak typing.

Colemak was published in 2006 as a middle path between QWERTY and Dvorak. It keeps the common shortcut keys Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY places and changes only 17 keys, so the switch is far gentler than Dvorak while still putting the most-used letters under your fingers.

On the same English passage, Colemak keeps about 73% of letters on the home row (QWERTY is near 36%) and cuts repeated same-finger presses to roughly 1.5%, versus about 7.9% on QWERTY. Less finger travel usually means more comfort over long sessions; it does not guarantee a higher top speed, which still depends mostly on practice.

Set your operating system input to Colemak first, otherwise you would be typing QWERTY characters while looking at a Colemak keyboard. Start with short two-to-five minute sessions and resist looking at your hands — the finger guide and on-screen keyboard exist to replace that habit.

Expect your speed to drop well below your QWERTY speed for the first week or two; that is the switch cost, not a verdict on Colemak. Track accuracy here before speed, because accuracy recovers first and speed follows it. Compare Colemak with Dvorak and QWERTY on the keyboard layouts page.

faq.q: Does this test switch my keyboard to Colemak?
faq.a: No. The test only shows a Colemak keyboard on this page. You switch your own operating system input to Colemak in its keyboard or language settings, and the test then scores whatever characters your layout produces.

faq.q: Do I need an account or to install anything?
faq.a: No. The Colemak keyboard is drawn by the page itself, the test runs entirely in your browser, and your results are stored only in this browser.

faq.q: Is Colemak easier to learn than Dvorak?
faq.a: For most QWERTY typists, yes. Colemak changes only 17 keys and keeps Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY positions, so common shortcuts and much of your muscle memory still apply. Dvorak moves almost every key.

faq.q: Will my Colemak WPM be lower than my QWERTY WPM at first?
faq.a: Yes, usually much lower for the first week or two while you rebuild muscle memory. Measure accuracy first; once accuracy returns to your normal level, speed follows.

faq.q: Which keys does Colemak move?
faq.a: Colemak keeps the bottom row's Z X C V B and the Q W A positions, and remaps the rest so E, T, N, S, I, R and O land on the home row. The full relabelling is drawn on the on-screen keyboard above.

faq.q: Can I switch back to QWERTY or try Dvorak here?
faq.a: Yes. The keyboard toolbar has a QWERTY / Dvorak / Colemak switch and your choice is remembered in this browser, so the same page works for any of the three layouts.

pages.title: Keyboard Layouts Compared - QWERTY vs Dvorak vs Colemak
pages.metaDesc: QWERTY vs Dvorak vs Colemak vs Workman compared: home-row use, finger travel and same-finger rate in one table. Test each free.
pages.heroP: QWERTY, Dvorak, Colemak and Workman compared on home-row use, finger travel and same-finger presses — so you can see which keyboard layout fits you before you commit weeks to switching. Try any of them on the test below with a layout-matched on-screen keyboard and finger guide.

seo.h2: QWERTY vs Dvorak vs Colemak vs Workman
p: A keyboard layout is just the map of which letter sits under each key. QWERTY has been the default since the 1870s, but alternative layouts rearrange the letters so the most common ones sit on the home row, cutting finger travel. Here is how the four best-known layouts compare on the same English text.

LayoutIntroducedFinger travel*Home-row useSame-finger
QWERTY1870s153 m (baseline)36%7.9%
Dvorak193688 m (−42%)71%3.2%
Colemak200689 m (−42%)73%1.5%
Workman201084 m (−45%)67%2.0%

Home-row share and same-finger figures below are modelled from a fixed English passage. For the documented history and design intent of each layout, see keyboard layout, Dvorak keyboard layout (patented 1936) and Colemak (released 2006, 74% of typing on the home row against 32% for QWERTY).

There is no single best layout, because less finger movement is not the same as faster typing. QWERTY wins on familiarity: it is on every shared computer and every shortcut assumes it. Dvorak alternates hands the most (about 67% of keystrokes), which many typists find rhythmic for long English prose. Colemak keeps the most letters on the home row (73%) and the fewest awkward same-finger presses (1.5%) while leaving Z, X, C, V and most shortcuts in place, so it is the usual pick for QWERTY users who want to switch. Workman trims total finger travel the most by also minimising sideways stretches.

For almost everyone, practice and accuracy move your WPM far more than the layout does. A fast QWERTY typist will beat a beginner on any layout. Switch for comfort and reduced finger travel, not for a guaranteed speed jump.

Switching costs you one to four weeks of slower, deliberate typing while new muscle memory forms, and shared or public machines will still be QWERTY. The payoff is less finger travel and, for many people, more comfort in long sessions. It is worth it mainly if you type a lot of English every day and own the keyboards you use most.

If you want the gentlest change, start with Colemak because it keeps your common shortcuts. If you love hand-alternation, try Dvorak. The honest answer for casual typists is that staying on QWERTY and practising is the higher-return move.

You can practise two of these layouts right now with a matching on-screen keyboard and finger guide: take the Colemak typing test or the Dvorak typing test, or measure your current speed on QWERTY with the main typing speed test. Each shows WPM, accuracy, consistency and a per-key heatmap so you can compare how a layout feels for you.
Layout decisions: Dvorak vs QWERTY — evidence, retraining cost, and who should switch.

faq.q: Which keyboard layout is the fastest?
faq.a: No layout is reliably fastest for everyone. Modeling shows Dvorak, Colemak and Workman cut finger travel by roughly 42 to 45% versus QWERTY, but measured typing speed depends far more on practice and accuracy than on the layout. The world's fastest typists use several different layouts, including QWERTY.

faq.q: Is Dvorak better than QWERTY?
faq.a: Dvorak puts about 71% of letters on the home row versus QWERTY's 36% and alternates hands more, which many typists find more comfortable for long English text. Studies show modest speed gains at best, so the main benefit is reduced finger movement and comfort, not a guaranteed speed jump.

faq.q: Is Colemak better than Dvorak?
faq.a: Colemak keeps more letters on the home row (about 73%) and the lowest same-finger rate (about 1.5%), and it changes only 17 keys while keeping Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY places, so it is easier to switch to than Dvorak. Dvorak alternates hands more. Which feels better is personal.

faq.q: What is the best keyboard layout for programming?
faq.a: Code uses far more punctuation, brackets and symbols than English prose, so prose-optimised layouts help less. Programmer variants such as Programmer Dvorak and Workman Programmer rearrange the number and symbol rows. Many developers stay on QWERTY because editors, shortcuts and pair-programming all assume it.

faq.q: How long does it take to switch keyboard layouts?
faq.a: Most people reach usable speed again in one to four weeks of short daily practice, and return to their old speed over one to three months. Accuracy recovers before raw speed, so track accuracy first.

faq.q: Can I practise Dvorak and Colemak online for free?
faq.a: Yes. This site has a free Dvorak typing test and a free Colemak typing test, each with an on-screen keyboard relabelled to that layout and a matching finger guide, so you can practise and measure your WPM without installing anything.

pages.tldr: Keyboard layouts trade finger travel against retraining cost. QWERTY puts about 32 percent of typing on the home row; Colemak puts about 74 percent there and Dvorak a little less, while keeping most shortcuts where your hands already expect them. Layout changes rarely beat consistent practice in the short term, so switch only if the travel figures matter more to you than the three to six weeks of slower typing a switch costs.
